systems.name: Multi-channel short-form video production pipeline
systems.decision: Creating short vertical videos for several YouTube channels can become repetitive and inconsistent when people must manually choose images and render every episode. This system prevents manual render-stage work, repeated shots across channels, repeated closing promises, and incorrect image rotation from reaching the finished video.
systems.what_it_does: This system turns source images into finished vertical short-form videos. A pipeline is a series of automated steps that pass work from one stage to the next. A vision model is an image-reading program that chooses a suitable frame using the written episode instructions, and ffmpeg is a command-line tool that assembles images, sound, timing, and video into a final file. Each channel has separate instructions, voice settings, and image supply rules so the channels can remain distinct.
mechanism: First, the SOURCE stage gathers possible images for each required shot. A shot is one planned visual moment in a video. Each shot need has its own search questions so different moments do not accidentally receive the same image candidates.
Next, PREFILTER removes or rejects unsuitable source images before selection. This reduces the chance that the selection step spends time considering obviously unusable images.
ROTCHECK corrects or checks image rotation before an image is selected. This order matters because selecting an image before fixing its orientation could cause the wrong version to be chosen.

SELECT gives the written brief and candidate images to qwen3-vl-235b. A model is a trained computer program, and this vision model can inspect images and compare them with the brief. It chooses one frame for each shot need.

CROP converts the selected image into the vertical 9:16 shape required for the short video. VERIFY runs quality checks, called QA gates, before rendering. A QA gate is a rule that must pass before work can continue.
BUILD uses ffmpeg to create the final video. The fixed order is enforced by the main runner script, and the order matters because rendering before checks would allow known problems into the output.

systems.name: Cron orchestration layer with append-only verification ledger
systems.decision: Some scheduled jobs were failing without making it clear whether they had run and failed or had never run at all. This system prevents that specific loss of evidence by recording a separate result for each expected job run.
systems.what_it_does: A cron job is a task that a computer starts at a planned time, and each of the 18 jobs first passes through a small script that gives the run a known name. An orchestrator is a program that checks whether the expected jobs are running, and a registry is a list of those expected jobs. A ledger is a record that only adds new entries, so this system writes one JSONL record, meaning one JSON object per line, for each observed job outcome. The system can repair a drifted copy of one document, sends a notification only when the overall condition changes, and returns exit code 0 when healthy or 1 when not healthy.
mechanism: First, every scheduled job is routed through the common runner script with the job name as its first argument. This gives later checks one consistent name for identifying the job.
Next, the runner records whether that named job actually started and what happened during the run. This matters because a failed run must leave different evidence from a run that never started.

The orchestrator then compares the registry, which lists the jobs that should exist, with the append-only ledger, which records what actually happened. Comparing the expected list with the recorded outcomes exposes both missing runs and failed runs.

For each check, the system adds a new per-run result instead of overwriting an older result. Keeping old entries makes the history reviewable and prevents a later status from hiding an earlier failure.
If the document mirror has drifted, the orchestrator repairs that one known repairable problem. It does not claim to repair every possible job failure.
The system compares the current health state with the previous health state before sending a notification. This order prevents repeated messages about the same unchanged problem.
Finally, it returns 0 for a healthy check and 1 for an unhealthy check. This lets another program or service detect the result without reading the detailed ledger.

systems.name: Posting quality gates A to E
systems.decision: Several publishing channels could accidentally release posts with repeated subjects, reused closing promises, copied descriptions, weak results, or the wrong speaking style. This system prevents those specific mistakes from reaching a channel when the relevant checks are actually run.
systems.what_it_does: This system is a set of five named checks, called gates, that inspect a proposed post before publishing. A gate is a rule that can approve or refuse an item. The checks compare performance data, subjects, closing promises, affiliate text, channel voice, and speaking speed against required rules. Four gates are connected to the publishing workflow, while the fifth is defined but not actually enforced in the tested loop.
mechanism: Gate A checks the known ratio for the brief. A ratio is a measured result compared with a required baseline. If the ratio is below 1.0, the brief is refused because it does not meet the minimum performance rule.

Gate B checks whether the subject has already been used and whether the closing promise has already been spent. A closing promise is the final invitation or expected next action in a post. Refusing repeats protects the publishing schedule from reusing the same idea or ending.

Gate C follows the chain of available closing promises and ranks tied choices by lift. Lift means the measured improvement or response associated with an option. This gate is used to choose among acceptable options rather than simply accepting every option.

Gate D creates the affiliate description when the required information is available. If the description cannot be created, it records the precise reason the affiliate check failed instead of silently allowing the item through.

Gate E checks the channel's assigned expressive voice preset and its words-per-second pacing band. A voice preset is a stored set of speaking-style choices, and words per second measures how quickly narration is spoken. The documented loop for this gate has no assertion body, so it does not currently enforce the check there.

The publishing scripts call Gates A and B during queue creation and call Gate D for affiliate descriptions. The source description does not show a publishing-path call for Gate C or an executed per-channel loop for Gate E.

systems.name: Multi-model LLM gateway with budget, cache and spend ceiling
systems.decision: Different tasks used to contact language models directly, so repeated requests could spend money again and there was no single record of what happened. This system prevents uncontrolled spending, missing records, incorrect routing, and accepting a response that used reasoning effort but returned no usable answer.
systems.what_it_does: This system is a central program that sends every language model request through one controlled route. A language model is software that reads messages and produces text, while an endpoint is the network service that receives the request. The system chooses a model and service, can use a saved answer instead of making the request again, checks spending limits, records the result, and can retry one known temporary provider failure. It also keeps provider information separate from user-maintained routing decisions so an automatic catalogue update does not replace a deliberate local choice.
mechanism: First, a caller sends a request to the gateway instead of contacting a model service directly. This order matters because the gateway can apply the same checks and record keeping to every request.

Next, the gateway identifies the requested job, such as research or drafting, and resolves it to a primary model and possibly a fallback model. A primary model is the first model tried, and a fallback is a replacement used when the first route cannot complete the job. This keeps routing decisions in one place.

If the caller supplied a specific model, the gateway uses that model's own provider and endpoint rather than looking it up as if it belonged to another provider. This prevents a valid model override from being sent to the wrong service.

Before contacting a provider, the gateway creates a SHA-256 cache key from the model, messages, and request settings. SHA-256 is a repeatable method for turning those inputs into a fixed fingerprint. If the fingerprint already has an answer, the gateway returns the saved answer, which prevents an identical request from spending money twice.

If there is no cached answer, the gateway estimates the request cost and compares it with the per-call budget. It refuses the request when the estimate is above the allowed amount, before provider usage occurs.

The gateway then reads the day's previous costs from its ledger and checks the daily cumulative cap. A ledger is a local record of events, and a cumulative cap is a maximum total for the day. This check comes after the per-call check because both the individual request and the day's total must be safe.

The gateway sends an approved request to the selected endpoint. For the specified kie.ai Claude route, it retries a temporary provider error with a bounded backoff, meaning it waits for a limited amount of time between a limited number of attempts. This handles a temporary failure without retrying forever.

When a response arrives, the gateway checks for a reasoning burn. This is a response where the completion token count equals the reasoning token count and the visible content is empty. Tokens are pieces of text counted by the model service. The gateway quarantines this result instead of treating it as a successful answer.

Finally, the gateway stores the request outcome, token counts, cost, and endpoint in the ledger, and stores the usable response in the cache when appropriate. Recording happens after the result is known so the record can describe what actually occurred.

systems.name: Local capability-search index over measured model findings
systems.decision: People previously chose a model for an unclear task from memory, while evidence about past model performance was spread across notes and conversation records. This system prevents an old, dead, or poorly supported model from being selected simply because someone remembered it or found its name in an unrelated file.
systems.what_it_does: This system searches evidence about what models are good at, rather than merely searching for files. It combines ordinary word matching with semantic matching, which means it can find text that has a similar meaning even when it uses different words. It represents text as an embedding, a list of numbers that summarizes meaning, and compares those lists to rank possible matches. It also records when a model is stale, meaning known to be unavailable or replaced, so that search results can warn against using it.
mechanism: First, the system gathers four evidence sources: personal notes, session transcripts, verified findings, and the current kie.ai model catalogue. A source is simply the kind of record from which information was taken. Keeping the sources separate helps show where a finding came from.

Next, it divides the source material into 280 smaller chunks. A chunk is a searchable piece of text. Smaller pieces make it easier to connect a specific task to the relevant evidence instead of returning an entire long record.

For each chunk, the system stores ordinary searchable text information for BM25 matching. BM25 is a scoring method that gives higher scores when the important words in a query appear in a relevant chunk, while reducing the importance of words that appear everywhere.

The system also turns each chunk into an embedding with all-MiniLM-L6-v2. An embedding is a list of numbers representing the text's meaning, and this model produces 384 numbers for each chunk. This second method helps find related wording that does not share the exact same terms.

When someone asks which model fits a job, the system compares the request with the indexed chunks using word matching and embedding similarity. It then ranks evidence about model capability rather than returning only matching filenames.

The system checks its stale markers while presenting findings. A stale marker records that a model should not be trusted for routing, along with why it was marked and when. This step matters after retrieval because a strong text match is still unsafe if the matching model is known to be dead.

When the underlying notes or catalogue change, a rebuild command recreates the local index without a network call. Rebuilding after source changes keeps search results aligned with the stored evidence, while avoiding an unnecessary external request.

systems.name: Browser MCP automation broker with isolated browser sessions
systems.decision: A computer program needed to control a real web browser, but giving an AI every available browser action would make the list of choices too large. The system prevents the AI from choosing the wrong browser action because it uses a small public tool list and checks web elements through the browser's accessibility tree instead of trusting text read from an image.
systems.what_it_does: This system is a browser automation broker, meaning a small service that receives simple requests and sends them to a larger browser-control system. The AI sees 4 tools, while the broker can internally select from 44 Playwright actions. Playwright is a library that controls a web browser. The system also keeps 29 browser profiles, where a profile is a separate set of browser settings and stored website data, and uses a pinned Chromium build, which is a fixed browser version, for compatibility. It can run without displaying a browser window, called headless mode, and checks the browser's accessibility tree, which is a structured description of page elements used by assistive technology, before clicking.
mechanism: First, the AI receives only 4 broker tools instead of the full set of 44 browser actions. This keeps the choice list small and reduces the chance that the AI selects an unsuitable low-level action.

Next, the broker translates the selected request into one of the 44 internal Playwright actions. Playwright is the software library that performs actions such as opening pages, clicking, typing, and uploading files.
The browser runs with a fixed Chromium build. Chromium is the browser engine, and keeping its version fixed matters because changing the browser version can make stored browser data unreadable.

When the system needs to identify a page element, it reads the accessibility tree first. This tree gives each usable element a structured identity, so the system can click the identified element rather than clicking based only on words recognized from a screenshot.

Before using a paid model to interpret a page, the system performs free, repeatable checks first. This observation ladder matters because simple checks can solve easy cases without spending money or adding uncertainty.
The browser can run in headless mode, meaning no visible browser window is drawn. This reduces memory use when a person does not need to watch the browser.

systems.name: Unified scoped event log and vector index across chat clients
systems.decision: Different chat programs stored their records separately, so a decision made in one program was difficult to find in another. The system prevents cross-project results from being mistaken for current-project evidence by attaching a scope label and applying scope filtering in the database.
systems.what_it_does: This system stores events, which are records of actions or messages, in one append-only database, meaning new records are added without rewriting old records. It also stores searchable numerical representations called vectors, which allow related text to be found by meaning rather than exact wording. Each record has a scope, meaning a label for the project or system it belongs to. Five tools are available to chat clients, while three maintenance operations are kept in a local command-line program, which is a text-based tool used by an operator.
mechanism: First, each client sends an event to the shared event store. An event is a record such as a tool call, decision, or message, and the shared store prevents each client from keeping an isolated history.
Next, the event receives a scope label. A scope identifies the project or broader area that the event belongs to.

The database applies scope filtering before returning results. This order matters because filtering in the database is more dependable than asking a language model to ignore unrelated results after they have already been retrieved.
The system also creates vectors for selected text. A vector is a list of numbers that represents the meaning or characteristics of text, allowing a similarity search to find related wording.

A watcher service drains the capture queue, which is a waiting list of events. A separate vector worker creates embeddings, meaning numerical text representations, so recording events and calculating search data do not block each other.

The five normal tools remain available through MCP, which is a standard way for an AI client to call external tools. Three maintenance tools stay in the local command-line program because registering them permanently would add unnecessary tool descriptions to every request.
Search results include their source scope, including when a search crosses scopes. This makes the origin visible instead of hiding it.

systems.name: Local code-search MCP with a rebuilt embedding stack
systems.decision: A code-search service stopped connecting because its software took too long to start and one search library was incompatible with the computer's graphics software. The system prevents silent empty search results by pinning compatible dependencies and using a smaller graphics-card batch size.
systems.what_it_does: This system searches source code by converting code chunks into vectors and comparing them with a FAISS index. FAISS is a library for fast similarity search, and an index is a data structure that organizes searchable vectors. The index uses 768 numerical dimensions, meaning each code chunk is represented by 768 numbers, and uses IndexFlatIP, which compares vectors using inner product similarity. The system uses EmbeddingGemma 300M, a 300-million-parameter model that turns text into vectors, on a graphics processor. Its software versions are pinned, meaning fixed to tested ranges, and the searchable index is stored outside the Python environment so rebuilding the environment does not delete it.
mechanism: First, the system pins the main software versions. A dependency is a library required by another program, and version pinning prevents an automatic update from changing behavior unexpectedly.
Next, it uses the CPU version of FAISS at 1.9.0.post1. FAISS is the search library, and the CPU version avoids relying on an incompatible graphics-specific wheel for the index operation.
The codebase is divided into chunks. A chunk is a smaller section of a file that can be represented and searched independently.
EmbeddingGemma 300M converts each chunk into a vector with 768 dimensions. The model must create these vectors before similarity search can work.
The model processes 4 chunks at a time on the graphics processor. A batch is the group processed in one operation, and the smaller batch avoids exhausting the available graphics memory.
The vectors are placed in an IndexFlatIP index. IndexFlatIP compares a query vector with stored vectors using inner product, a mathematical similarity score.

When a user searches, the query is converted into the same kind of vector and compared with the stored vectors. Using the same representation for both sides matters because otherwise the similarity scores would not be meaningful.
The index is stored outside the software environment. This means rebuilding the environment can replace libraries without rebuilding the entire searchable data set.

systems.name: Brand-consistency factorial experiment with a reference image
systems.decision: The question was whether showing a reference image and using a carefully structured prompt help an image model reproduce a brand wordmark correctly. This experiment prevents conclusions based only on a few attractive examples or on personal visual impressions.
systems.what_it_does: This system creates images under four combinations: a plain prompt or a structured prompt, each with or without a reference image. A prompt is the written instruction given to the image model, and a reference image is an example image supplied to guide the result. It checks the generated images with OCR, which means software that reads text from pictures, and with CIEDE2000, a numerical measure of color difference. It then compares the groups using statistical tests, which estimate whether an observed difference is larger than would be expected from random variation.
mechanism: First, define a 2 by 2 factorial design. This means crossing two choices, prompt style and reference-image use, to create four conditions. Defining all four conditions first matters because it makes the comparison balanced and makes it possible to test whether the two choices interact.
Next, prepare nine briefs and generate 20 images for each condition and brief. A brief is one specific image task. Repeated images are needed because one generation can succeed or fail by chance.

Keep the confirmatory set fixed before looking at the comparison. Confirmatory means the main test chosen in advance, while exploratory means an additional analysis considered after or alongside the main test. Fixing the main set first reduces the chance of changing the question after seeing the results.
Score the wordmark with OCR exact match. An exact match means the text read from the image is exactly the required brand wordmark, rather than merely looking similar.
Measure color with CIEDE2000. This is a standardized calculation of how different two colors appear numerically, with a smaller distance generally meaning closer colors.

Do not calculate CLIP or FID for the final set, and record why they were not used. CLIP is a model-based similarity score between images and text or images. FID is a distribution-level comparison often used for generated images. Recording the omission makes it clear that these measurements are unavailable rather than accidentally forgotten.

Use a stratified test for the 2 by 2 design. Stratified means comparing results within defined groups, such as briefs or tiers, before combining them. This order helps preserve the factorial structure and prevents a pooled comparison from hiding an interaction between prompt style and reference-image use.
Report the confirmatory and exploratory results separately. This prevents a secondary result from being presented as though it were the preselected main result.

systems.name: Model robustness and failure-cause analysis
systems.decision: Different models were used different numbers of times, so simply comparing their raw failure counts could give a misleading result. This system prevents the specific failure of treating the number of attempts as if it were a fair sample size or treating every failure as the same kind of problem.
systems.what_it_does: This system records image-generation attempts made with four models and separates attempts that produced a usable scored result from attempts that did not. It groups failures by their cause for each model instead of reporting only one total failure number. A success rate is the share of scored attempts that succeeded, and a 95 percent confidence interval is a calculated range showing the uncertainty around that rate. The gpt model is used as the baseline, meaning the reference model against which the other models are compared. A stratified test compares models within matching model and condition groups, and the rejected alternative test is kept with the reason it was rejected.
mechanism: First, record every generation attempt and identify which model made it. This preserves the unequal number of attempts instead of hiding it.

Next, identify whether each attempt produced a scored cell, meaning an output for which the evaluation could be completed. This matters because an attempt without a scored result should not silently count as a normal success or failure.
Then, label the cause of each failure for each model. This shows whether models fail in different ways rather than making all failures look identical.

Calculate each model's success rate from the scored results and calculate a 95 percent confidence interval around it. The interval communicates uncertainty, so a small difference is not automatically treated as a reliable difference.
Use gpt as the baseline and compare every other model with it. A baseline gives all comparisons the same reference point.

Use Fisher exact test where a comparison involves small counts. This test checks whether the observed success and failure counts could reasonably differ by chance without relying on a large-sample approximation.

Use the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test across model and condition pairs. This combines comparisons while accounting for the condition groups, which is why it is preferred to a single ungrouped comparison here.
Record the statistical method that was rejected and why. This makes the analysis auditable and prevents a later reader from assuming that an unreported method was used.

systems.name: TermsGuard contractual clause compliance pipeline
systems.decision: Lawyers were spending time reviewing every flagged contract clause, including clauses that did not need attention. The system is meant to prevent important unfair clauses from being buried in a large amount of routine review work.
systems.what_it_does: This system examines contract clauses in two stages. First, a classifier, meaning a program that sorts text into categories, proposes which clauses may be concerning. Then Claude, a language model that reads text and produces a judgement, reviews up to 15 proposed clauses using relevant reference material. A retrieval index, meaning a searchable store of text fragments, finds supporting governance information. If the external model service is unavailable because no API key is set, the system still performs similarity matching and clearly reports that it did not receive a model verification.
mechanism: The system starts with 102 hand-labelled clauses, meaning clauses that a person has already marked as fair or unfair. These examples give the first-stage classifier concrete examples to compare against.

The classifier compares clauses with the reference examples and proposes clauses that may be unfair. This comes first because sending every clause to the language model would use more time and service capacity.

The system searches a FAISS index. FAISS is a tool for finding text with similar meaning, and the index contains 4,527 chunks of governance reference material. This adds relevant background before a final judgement is made.
The system sends no more than 15 proposed clauses to Claude. Limiting the number keeps the review step bounded and focuses the model on the clauses most likely to need attention.

The result is routed using confidence thresholds. A score of 0.55 or more is treated as high confidence, while a score of 0.45 or more is treated as medium confidence. The exact routing behaviour below those levels is not further specified here.

When no API key is available, the system switches to matching-only mode instead of stopping. Every response includes verification_source and verification_error, which identify where the result came from and whether an error occurred, so a fallback cannot appear to be a successful model ruling.

systems.name: Smart Medical Records Engine with per-patient retrieval
systems.decision: A clinical assistant could accidentally retrieve one patient's note while answering a question about another patient if both notes used similar words. The system is designed to prevent cross-patient record leakage.
systems.what_it_does: This is a clinical RAG system, meaning it retrieves relevant records and gives them to a language model to help form an answer. It makes the patient identifier part of the search boundary, rather than searching everyone and filtering results later. A local language model runs inside the hospital network, while authorization, redaction, and audit recording happen around the request. An audit log is a record of who requested information and what retrieval or answer activity occurred.
mechanism: A physician request is first checked for authorization. Authorization means checking that the person is allowed to access the requested patient's information.

The request is associated with a patient_id, which is the identifier for one patient. This identifier is included in the retrieval query itself, so records for other patients are excluded before similarity search returns results.
Each note stores a 768-number embedding beside its patient_id. An embedding is a numerical representation of meaning, and a vector is the ordered list of numbers used for similarity comparison.

PostgreSQL with pgvector searches the permitted patient's stored note vectors for relevant matches. PostgreSQL is the database, and pgvector is the database extension that supports vector similarity search.
PII redaction removes or hides personally identifying information where the application requires it. PII means information that can identify a person, such as a name or address.
The matching notes are passed to llama3.1 running through Ollama on the local network. This order keeps the records inside the hospital environment before the model generates an answer.
The system writes retrieval and answer events to an audit log. Recording these events makes later review possible and provides evidence of what the system did.
The API, database, model, and supporting parts run as four Docker Compose services on one private network. Docker Compose starts and connects these services in a controlled environment.

systems.name: Image QA gate over frozen ResNet50 Siamese features
systems.decision: An image-generation process could put the wrong person's identity into an image even when the pose looked correct. The gate is designed to prevent this dangerous false positive, meaning incorrectly accepting two different people as the same person.
systems.what_it_does: This system checks whether an image has the intended identity and whether its overall grade or quality fits the requirement. It uses a Siamese network, which compares two images by sending them through matching processing paths, on top of frozen ResNet50 features. ResNet50 is a pretrained image-recognition model, and frozen means its learned features are not changed during this task. The system makes an accept or reject decision using a threshold, which is a chosen score boundary.
mechanism: The system extracts visual features from images with ResNet50. Features are measurable patterns such as shapes and identity-related visual information, and using a pretrained model avoids learning all visual patterns from the beginning.

The Siamese network compares the features from the relevant image pair. Its two matching paths are intended to measure whether the images represent the same identity or satisfy the required relationship.

The gate checks two conditions rather than only one. Identity similarity must be high, and grade fit must be below its threshold, so an image with a good pose but the wrong person can still be rejected.

The decision threshold is selected using validation data. Validation data is data used to choose settings, and keeping the test data separate prevents the test result from being used to tune the system.

The threshold changes from 0.5 to 0.4821 after validation tuning. This happens before final evaluation so the reported test result measures the chosen rule rather than a rule adjusted after seeing the test answers.

The gate runs on a CPU, meaning a general-purpose processor rather than a graphics processor. This allows it to operate as an inline check during image processing instead of only as a later batch job.

systems.name: Customer Care BPMN triage agent
systems.decision: Customer-care tickets were being routed manually, and a wrong route could send a customer to a queue that could not help. The system is designed to prevent uncertain tickets from being forced into an unreliable automatic category.
systems.what_it_does: This system reads a customer-care ticket and predicts which category should handle it. It uses Naive Bayes, a simple statistical classifier that estimates categories from the words in the ticket. The workflow is shown as BPMN, a diagram format for business processes, so the automatic step and the human escalation step are visible. When the classifier is not confident enough, the ticket goes to a person instead of being automatically routed.
mechanism: The system starts with a labelled corpus of 210 tickets. A corpus is a collection of documents, and labelled means each ticket already has a known category for learning.

Naive Bayes learns how words are associated with each category. It is deliberately simple because the dataset is small and the business can more easily understand its decisions than a more complicated model.
For a new ticket, the classifier calculates a confidence score for its most likely category. This score expresses how strongly the available word evidence supports that category.

The system compares the score with 0.55. If the score is below 0.55, the ticket is sent to a human; this step matters because uncertainty is handled explicitly rather than hidden inside an automatic decision.

If the score meets the required confidence, the workflow routes the ticket to the predicted category. BPMN represents both paths so the process can be reviewed as a business workflow, not only as source code.
The prediction is evaluated on held-out tickets. Held-out means the tickets were kept out of training so the evaluation tests the model on examples it did not learn from.

metrics.explanation: The learning collection contains 210 categorised tickets, with 42 tickets assigned to each category.
metrics.proves: It proves the classifier was built from an evenly sized labelled collection of 210 examples.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that 42 examples per category are enough to represent real customer-care traffic.

metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove a 95.2 percent rate for future tickets because the test sample is small.

metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that 0.55 is the best threshold or that human decisions are always correct.

systems.name: Surge pricing policy comparison, reinforcement learning against a genetic algorithm
systems.decision: A ride-hailing pricing policy needed to be chosen between two learning methods, but the methods had to be compared fairly. The experiment is designed to prevent one method from appearing better merely because it received different data or random conditions.
systems.what_it_does: This system simulates pricing strategies using real Boston ride records as input data. It compares Q-learning, a method that learns actions from rewards over time, with a genetic algorithm, a method that improves a population of candidate policies through selection and variation. Several fixed strategies provide baselines, meaning reference methods for comparison. Each method is tested with the same number of seeds and simulated days so the comparison focuses on the method rather than accidental randomness.
mechanism: The system prepares 637,976 ride records and removes metered Taxi-tier rides because those records do not contain a quoted price for this experiment. This makes the input fit the pricing calculation.
It defines the reward as daily revenue. A reward is the numerical result that a learning method tries to improve, so both learning methods are judged using the same business objective.

The Q-learning agent observes a simulated situation and learns which pricing action tends to produce higher future rewards. The genetic algorithm instead creates candidate pricing policies and repeatedly keeps and varies the better-performing candidates.
The experiment also runs flat pricing and a third baseline. These reference strategies show what the learning methods achieve compared with simpler alternatives.

Every strategy is evaluated on the same 8 random seeds and 30 simulated days per seed. A seed is a fixed starting value for random number generation, so reusing the same seeds makes the comparison more consistent.
The global seed is set to 42. This makes the experiment reproducible, meaning another run with the same code and inputs can recreate the same random setup.

The report compares average daily revenue and average ride fare, then explains why one method performed better. Separating results from explanation helps distinguish the measured outcome from an interpretation of the outcome.

systems.name: Telecom CRM and call-record data migration programme
systems.decision: Customer information was stored in several business systems, and those systems sometimes disagreed about the same person or about the number of active customers. The work was designed to prevent incorrect, incomplete, or duplicated data from being trusted by reports and later systems.
systems.what_it_does: This is a set of data migration and checking processes for a telecom operator. A CRM, or customer relationship management system, is the system that stores customer information, and Python scripts copy that information into a cleaner format. SQL, a language for asking questions of stored data, compares the copied records with the original records to find missing or inconsistent data. KPI dashboards, which are screens showing important operational measurements, display more than 30 measures, while UAT, or user acceptance testing, checks whether the migrated data and related functions behave as expected.
mechanism: First, customer records are extracted from the CRM. Extraction means reading records from one system and preparing them for use elsewhere, and it happens first because later checks need a defined copy of the source data.
Next, Python scripts clean and validate the extracted records. Python is a programming language, and validation means checking whether data follows expected rules before other people rely on it.

Then, SQL compares the number of extracted rows with the number of rows in the source system. A row is one stored record, and this comparison happens after extraction so that missing records can be identified before reporting or migration continues.

The process checks for disagreements between systems, including duplicate identities. An identity is the set of information used to represent one customer, and a duplicate identity occurs when two systems represent the same customer with different keys, or identifying values.

The team worked with the solutions architect on a migration architecture for 400 million daily call records. A migration architecture is the planned design for moving and organizing data, and designing it before implementation matters because the size and daily volume affect how the data can be handled.

The validated information is used in KPI dashboards and in formal UAT. A dashboard is a visual display of measurements, and a test case is one documented check of expected behavior; testing after validation provides a structured way to find problems before users trust the result.

metrics.explanation: This measured the amount of staff time saved each week by using Python to extract CRM data instead of performing the same extraction manually. The unit is hours per week.

metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that every extracted record was correct, complete, or free of duplicate identities.

systems.name: Outreach verification and audit database
systems.decision: Sending an outreach message with an unchecked claim about a company or product can damage the sender's credibility. This system prevents factual claims from being treated as verified without a recorded check and prevents suppressed or opted-out contacts from being selected through ordinary queue views.
systems.what_it_does: This system is a customer relationship management database, meaning a structured store of information about contacts, research, and messages. It stores contacts, audits, findings, claim checks, opt-outs, planned posts, and outreach events in SQLite, a small database format. Each claim in a message gets its own record showing whether it was checked. Database views are saved queries that present only records meeting specific rules, such as contacts that are not suppressed.
mechanism: First, the database stores a contact record. A contact is a potential contact, and the record gives the system one place to track that contact's status.

An audit then records a review of the contact or company. An audit finding is one individual result from that review. Keeping findings in a separate table allows one audit to contain many findings without repeating the audit information.

Each factual statement planned for an outreach message becomes a claim check. The claim check stores the statement and its verification state, such as checked or still needing verification. This creates a record before sending rather than relying on memory.

Opt-out and suppression information is stored and exposed through views. An opt-out means the person has asked not to receive messages, while suppression means the system should exclude the contact. Using views makes the same exclusion rule available wherever the contact queue is read.
The posting schedule records what is planned, while outreach events record what was actually sent or attempted. Keeping these separate prevents a plan from being mistaken for a completed message.

systems.name: Cross-model image bakeoff with defect capture
systems.decision: Choosing an image model based on reputation can miss how it behaves on the exact task that matters. This system prevents the specific failure of selecting a model that looks attractive in general but produces incorrect product details or text in the required image.
systems.what_it_does: This system gives several image-generation models the same product image task and the same expected result. It records the task identifier, the usage credits spent, and the time taken for each run. People inspect the resulting images directly, because an optical character recognition tool, which tries to read text in an image, can give a low score even when the text looks correct to a person. The review names the exact defect, such as mirrored or reversed small text, instead of using only a general failure label. The winner is selected using both text accuracy and similarity to the product, rather than appearance alone.
mechanism: Start with the same product shot, wordmark, and expectation set for each candidate model. Keeping the input and requirement fixed makes the comparison about the models rather than changing tasks.
Run the image request for each candidate and record the task identifier, credits spent, and wall time. Wall time means the elapsed time from starting the request to receiving the result.
Inspect each output visually. This step is necessary because an automated text-reading score may disagree with what a person can actually see.
Name the defect precisely when one appears. For example, mirrored text is text that is reversed left to right, which is different from text that is merely misspelled or unreadable.

Compare the models on text fidelity and product match. Text fidelity means whether the required words and their orientation are correct, while product match means whether the generated object still resembles the intended product.
Choose the model that performs best on those requirements, while retaining the cost and time information for the practical tradeoff.
Record competitors that are unavailable on the chosen vendor separately from models that were tested. This prevents an unavailable option from being mistaken for a poor-performing tested option.

metrics.explanation: A recorded run produced 3 images. Each image used 6 credits, the available balance decreased from 816 credits to 798 credits, and each image took between 66 and 71 seconds to complete.

systems.name: Multi-model audition panel for generated hero selection
systems.decision: One selected hero image is reused in roughly 300 later image generations, so a poor first choice can affect a large batch of work. This system prevents the specific failure of choosing a hero from one opinion or choosing an image with lighting or appearance that creates unwanted defects in every downstream result.
systems.what_it_does: This system creates 42 candidate hero images, with one candidate based on each mood-board source image. Four independent judge models each select and rank their top three candidates. Their choices are saved in a verdict file that records first, second, and third choices and counts how often each candidate was mentioned. Every candidate uses the same technical frame, meaning the same controlled image setup, so inherited lighting does not unfairly influence later images. The casting is left open so the image system invents a face instead of copying a real person's likeness, and the extraction format has no field for storing a likeness.
mechanism: Generate one candidate for each of the 42 mood-board source images. This creates a broad set of alternatives before selecting a hero.

Keep the technical frame fixed for every candidate. A fixed frame controls the camera and lighting conditions, so one candidate does not receive an accidental advantage or introduce a directional shadow that later images will copy.
Ask four judge models to review the same candidate set independently. Independent judging reduces the risk that one judge's choice becomes the only opinion.
Have each judge record a first, second, and third choice. Ranking more than one choice preserves useful information when several candidates are acceptable.
Save the rankings in a standing verdict file and count mentions across judges. A mention count is the number of times a candidate appears in the judges' selected positions.
Use agreement among the judges to identify the leading candidate. Strong agreement is a clearer selection signal than a single isolated preference.
Keep the casting open and omit any field that could store a copied likeness. This makes the intended result an invented face rather than a stored identity reference.
Mark later authoritative rounds as replacing earlier rounds when the source record says they were superseded. This prevents an outdated selection from being treated as the final decision.

metrics.explanation: The system created and evaluated 42 different possible hero images. A candidate is one proposed image that could be selected for later use.

systems.name: Longitudinal experiment evidence log with a validator
systems.decision: Research decisions and disagreements between numerical scores and human visual judgment were being reconstructed from memory after the work happened. This system prevents a later summary from silently changing what was observed, when it was observed, or how certain the observation was.
systems.what_it_does: This system records research observations as individual lines of structured text. Each line includes the kind of observation, a confidence level, and a timestamp. It marks whether an observation was captured live or reconstructed later, and it keeps a separate automatic record of media-generation calls. A validator checks the records for formatting errors and broken pieces before the log is used for the research write-up.
mechanism: Record each observation as one JSONL line. JSONL means JSON objects stored one per line, so each observation can be added, checked, and processed separately without rewriting the whole file.

Include the observation kind, confidence, and timestamp. The kind says what sort of event was recorded, confidence says how certain the recorder is, and the timestamp says when it was recorded. Keeping these fields together preserves context for later review.

Mark live captures separately from backfilled reconstructions. A live capture is written close to the event, while a backfilled reconstruction is written later from memory or other evidence. This distinction prevents a later recollection from appearing to be contemporaneous evidence.

Capture generation calls automatically using a directory marker. A generation call is a request made to create media, and a directory marker is a known location or label that tells the logging system which calls belong to the experiment. Automatic capture reduces dependence on someone remembering to make a manual note.

Run the validator against the observation log. The validator is a checking program that looks for missing or malformed fields and broken shards, where a shard is a separated piece of stored log data. This catches structural problems before the records are treated as evidence.
Use the log as the main source for the thesis write-up. This order matters because the written conclusions are based on dated records rather than on a summary created after the outcome is known.

systems.name: Flask image generation studio with streaming job updates
systems.decision: Image generation can take time, so a user needs to see what is happening instead of waiting for a blank loading screen. The application is also designed to prevent invalid uploads and incorrect handling of a reference image.
systems.what_it_does: This is a Flask web application, meaning a Python program that serves pages and handles web requests. It starts an image-generation job and streams status lines to the browser as the job progresses. Streaming means sending updates as they are produced rather than waiting for the final result. The application also checks uploaded file types and converts local file locations into URLs that a remote interface can use.
mechanism: The user submits an image-generation request through the web interface. Flask receives the request and starts the related generation work.

The backend runs the generation process as a subprocess, meaning a separate operating-system process. It reads output one line at a time so progress can be sent to the user while the job is still running.
The browser receives each progress line as it becomes available. This order matters because the user can see intermediate stages instead of receiving only a final success or failure message.

When generation produces a file on the local machine, the application translates its local path into a tunnel URL. A URL is an address the remote browser can request, while a local path is meaningful only on the machine that created the file.
Before saving an upload, the application checks that its file type is allowed. This reduces the chance that unsupported or unwanted files enter the workflow.
The application includes a regression test for a reference-image defect. A regression test is a repeatable check that confirms a previously fixed problem does not return after later code changes.

systems.name: Episode-level QA gates for brief, claims and frames
systems.decision: A video episode could look complete after rendering while still containing bad frames, mismatched narration, unsupported claims, an invalid script, or a malformed brief. This system prevents those specific problems from being discovered only after upload by checking the episode before it is published.
systems.what_it_does: This system is a group of checks for an episode, meaning one completed video and its supporting files. It checks the brief, narration script, factual claims, the connection between narration and shots, and the selected images or frames. A frame is one still image from a video, and a shot is a timed section of the video that uses one or more frames. The checks also compare shot timing with the audio so the pictures and spoken words do not drift apart.
mechanism: The brief check examines the collection of planned episode information and confirms that it has the format the pipeline expects. A pipeline is an ordered set of processing steps that turns inputs into an output.
The script check examines the narration before rendering. Narration is the spoken text of the episode. Checking it early allows script errors to be rejected before time is spent generating video.

The claims check examines factual statements in the script and affiliate description. A claim is a statement presented as true. This check is intended to identify unsupported or invalid statements before publication.
The frame check examines selected images for duplication and quality rules. It uses SHA-256 hashing, which creates a repeatable digital fingerprint from an image, to detect identical frames.

The beat-alignment check compares each shot with the narration beat it was designed to illustrate. A beat is a small intended idea or moment in the narration. This ordering matters because a technically valid image can still be wrong for the words being spoken.

The timing check requires each shot to last from 0.4 seconds to 5.0 seconds, requires the final shot to last no more than 4.0 seconds, and requires the total shot time to be within 0.6 seconds of the audio. These checks run before upload so timing failures can be corrected before viewers see them.

metrics.explanation: Each shot must last at least 0.4 seconds and no more than 5.0 seconds. The final shot has a stricter maximum of 4.0 seconds. The sum of shot durations may differ from the audio duration by no more than 0.6 seconds. SHA-256 fingerprints are compared to find identical frames.
metrics.proves: The system has explicit shot-length, final-shot, audio-alignment, and duplicate-frame rules.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the narration is factually correct, that the imagery is semantically appropriate, or that every episode passes.

metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that all four helpers are executed, correct, or sufficient for accurate alignment.

systems.name: MCP reconnect watchdog for self-healing tool servers
systems.decision: When a local tool server stopped, the main program marked it as failed and left it stopped until a person changed a configuration file. This system prevents that specific failure from requiring manual recovery when the expected transport error is written to the log.
systems.what_it_does: MCP is a way for a main program to communicate with tool servers, which are smaller programs that provide specific capabilities. A watchdog is a background program that watches for a known failure signal, and here it watches the main program's log, which is a record of events and errors. When it sees the relevant transport error, it changes a restart marker in the settings for the affected server. The main program notices that setting change and starts the server again, while a 15 second cooldown prevents repeated changes during the restart.
mechanism: First, a system service, meaning a background program managed by the operating system, follows the main program's log. Watching the log provides direct evidence that a communication failure occurred.

The watchdog waits for a line that specifically reports an MCP transport error. A transport error means that communication between the main program and the tool server failed, and using this signal avoids restarting a server merely because it is still starting.

When the matching error appears, the watchdog increases the affected server's restart marker in both relevant configuration files. A configuration file is a settings file, and the marker is a value whose change tells the main program that a restart is requested.
The main program watches its configuration and sees that the marker changed. It then stops treating the server as permanently failed and respawns it, meaning it starts a new server process.

The watchdog waits 15 seconds before allowing another marker change for the same recovery sequence. This order matters because the server may still be restarting, and repeated changes could cause restart loops or marker ping-pong.

The recovery was tested by deliberately stopping the code-search server and checking that the error appeared, the marker changed, and the server returned without a person editing the settings. This test checks the complete chain rather than only one component.

metrics.value: verified end to end: SIGTERM to the code-search server produced a transport error, the watchdog bumped the marker and opencode respawned the server with no human intervention
metrics.explanation: This records one complete test. SIGTERM is an operating-system request to stop a program; the test confirmed that stopping the server caused a communication error, triggered the watchdog, changed the restart marker, and caused the main program to start the server again without a person intervening.
metrics.proves: This directly supports that the tested recovery sequence worked from forced server termination through automatic restart.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove recovery for every possible failure, every server, repeated failures, or long-term reliability.

metrics.value: 7 of 8 servers tolerate the restart marker argument without any code change; code-search needed one patch to strip the flag before argparse
metrics.explanation: Seven out of eight servers can receive the restart marker information without changes to their code. The code-search server required one code change to remove the extra flag before argparse, which is the Python tool that reads command-line options.
metrics.proves: This directly supports the stated compatibility result for eight servers and identifies the one server that needed a change.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that all eight servers recover successfully in every situation or that the required code change has no side effects.

systems.honest_limit: The evidence validates one forced-stop recovery and reports compatibility for eight servers, but it does not measure recovery time, recovery success over many trials, behavior during repeated failures, or failures that do not produce the expected log line. The system depends on the main program noticing the configuration change and on the server accepting the restart information.
systems.status_note: A transport failure was used to verify automatic recovery on code-search.

systems.name: Narration-driven episode analysis autopilot
systems.decision: Planning the images for an episode used to require a person to read the narration and decide what shots were needed. This system prevents the process from silently using the same image search for every shot and prevents a mismatch between the narration timing and the written visual plan.
systems.what_it_does: This system starts with the spoken script and turns it into a visual plan. It transcribes the narration, meaning it converts spoken audio into written words, and divides those words into beats, where a beat is one small idea or section. It then maps each beat to shot needs and gives each need its own search questions. The builder checks that the number and timing of planned beats match the real narration before production continues.
mechanism: First, the narration is generated. Starting with narration matters because the visuals are meant to support what is actually said.
The narration is transcribed into text. Transcription creates a written version that later programs can inspect without a person listening to the whole recording.
The text is split into beats. Each beat represents one meaningful part of the narration, making it possible to plan a visual for each idea rather than treating the whole episode as one block.
The beats are mapped to shot needs. A shot need is a request for one visual moment, such as a particular subject, action, or setting.

Each shot need receives its own query list. A query is a search request used to find possible source images. This step is essential because using identical queries for every need caused the source stage to place the same candidate set in each folder and left many needs without usable selections.

The brief is written after the narration and beat count are known. The builder refuses a mismatch between the brief timings and the narration, so this order prevents a plan based on an incorrect number of beats.

If the database says the reel is already complete, the system skips it. This order matters because checking status before downloading avoids repeating work.
If the reel is not complete, the system downloads it. The downloaded file becomes the input for later steps.
The system extracts frames from the downloaded video and writes them to a dated folder. The date helps separate one processing run from another.
The system exports structured information as JSON and writes a log for each step. Logs are written records of what a program did, which makes troubleshooting possible when a step fails.
The database is updated with success or failure. Recording an error message makes the failure visible and lets a later run decide what needs attention.

systems.name: Mullay brand media generation pipeline
systems.decision: Brand imagery can look inconsistent when the wrong image model is used for a particular job or when prompts are based on guesswork. This system prevents one model from being used for every task and records practical rules learned from observed image failures.
systems.what_it_does: This system creates brand images from reference photos and produces related angle sheets and edits. It routes each job type to a chosen image model: flux-2 for creating a hero image from a reference, and gpt-image-2 for angle sheets and edits to an existing photo. Uploading a reference, creating a task, checking its progress, and downloading the result are separate steps so a failure can be located. The pipeline also records prompt and quality rules intended to improve face consistency and avoid background problems.
mechanism: The system identifies the job type first. A job type is the purpose of the image request, such as creating a main image, making several angles, or editing an existing photo.
For a hero capture from a reference, it routes the task to flux-2. Routing means choosing a particular model according to a rule rather than choosing one arbitrarily.
For an angle sheet or an edit of an existing photo, it routes the task to gpt-image-2. Keeping these choices separate matters because the source reports different models for different uses.

The system uploads the reference or source image, creates an image task, checks the task until it is ready, and downloads the result. Separating these steps makes it possible to tell whether failure happened during upload, task creation, waiting, or download.

It uses high quality settings because lower settings produced plastic-looking skin in observed tests. This is a practical configuration based on a measured failure, not a general claim about every image.

It places the face instruction early in the prompt and uses a grey background. These choices were adopted because earlier prompt terms receive more emphasis in the observed setup and white backgrounds were reported to bleed into the image.

A static site is a collection of already generated web files that can be served without running application code for each visitor. The generator applies one shared type scale, spacing rhythm, and color palette so pages follow the same design system. It also checks reduced-motion preferences and browser support before showing certain animations, while keeping the content visible when those features are unavailable.
mechanism: The generator reads project README files. A README is a project document containing descriptions and evidence that can be turned into page content.

It creates the site pages from that source information instead of relying on separately hand-edited pages. This order matters because one source reduces the chance that different pages tell conflicting stories.
The design system applies shared text sizes, spacing measurements, and colors. A design system is a set of repeated visual rules that keeps pages consistent.
Motion is placed behind a reduced-motion check. This check respects a visitor's request for less movement and prevents animation from being forced on that visitor.
Motion also requires an animation-timeline support check. A browser feature check asks whether the visitor's browser can perform the animation correctly.
If either check fails, the content remains visible without depending on the motion. This matters because unsupported animation should remove decoration, not the information itself.
The site is measured against performance targets for loading, interaction delay, and layout movement. These are targets, not proof that every visitor experiences those values.

systems.name: Local Real-ESRGAN 4K upscaling queue

systems.what_it_does: This system downloads images from a link queue and enlarges them locally using Real-ESRGAN. Real-ESRGAN is an image enlargement program that uses a trained model to create a higher-resolution version. The program uses the local graphics processor, called a GPU, and processes the image in 512-pixel tiles so large images can be handled in sections. A done ledger records success or failure, while a staging folder separates work in progress from completed output.

It places the source or working file in a staging area. A staging area is a temporary location for files that are not yet complete.

The program uses a tile size of 512 pixels. Tiling divides a large image into smaller sections so the GPU needs less memory at one time.

When processing finishes, the system writes the enlarged image to the output area and records the result in the done ledger. If processing fails, it records FAILED rather than pretending the item is complete.

systems.name: Multi-agent trading scan dashboard
systems.decision: A reinforcement-learning scan produced results that needed to be viewed without running the expensive training process again. The dashboard is designed to prevent users from needing a live server or a fresh training run just to inspect the latest stored results.
systems.what_it_does: This is a static dashboard, meaning a collection of web files that can display information without a continuously running application server. It reads a JSON file, which is a structured text format for data, containing the latest trading results. The results cover 36 assets and use different learning agents for different asset groups. The dashboard presents risk-adjusted results based on Sharpe ratio and includes a hidden Markov model signal, which is a statistical estimate of hidden market conditions.
mechanism: The training or scanning process produces a results file containing the latest measurements. The dashboard does not rerun that process when someone opens the page.
The page loads the JSON results file. JSON is used here as a simple, structured handoff between the process that produced the results and the page that displays them.
The system associates SAC, TD3, or PPO with each asset class. These are different reinforcement-learning methods, meaning methods that learn actions by receiving rewards from an environment.
The reward is based on Sharpe ratio. Sharpe ratio is a risk-adjusted measure that compares return with variability, so the learning objective considers both gain and risk rather than gain alone.

A hidden Markov model contributes a regime signal. This model estimates an underlying market state, such as a possible market condition, from observed data even though the state itself is not directly visible.
The browser displays the stored results as charts or tables. Because the page only reads the prepared file, it has no server dependency in the described setup.

systems.name: Personal site and links hub
systems.decision: Contact information and public profiles can be difficult to share when they are scattered across several services. This system prevents that information from depending on a single platform by placing links, a QR code, a contact file, and related assets in one static page.
systems.what_it_does: This system is a static links page, meaning the page is made from files that can be served directly without a running application. It includes a QR code, which is a square image that a phone can scan, a vCard contact file, which stores contact details in a format address books can import, and a wallpaper set. Git records changes to the public files over time.
mechanism: The system stores the page and its assets as ordinary static files. This keeps the runtime simple because the visitor's browser only needs to download and display the files.
It provides a QR code that points people toward the public contact surface. This gives a quick phone-based route without requiring someone to type a long address.
It provides a vCard file for contact details. A vCard lets a visitor save the information into a contacts application rather than copying each field by hand.
It includes the wallpaper set as another downloadable public asset. Keeping these assets with the page gives the public profile one consistent home.
Git tracks changes to the repository. This creates a history of edits and makes it possible to see when the public surface changed.

metrics.proves: It directly supports that the repository contains 38 recorded commits at the measurement point.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the page is popular, complete, secure, accessible, or currently working in every browser.

systems.name: Multi-agent MCP layer across eight servers
systems.decision: Several AI clients needed access to the same models, memory, code search, web lookup, and browser capabilities, but separate integrations could behave differently. The system prevents that integration drift by routing these capabilities through one shared tool protocol and by automatically restarting a failed server.
systems.what_it_does: This system is a shared MCP layer, where MCP is a standard protocol that lets an AI client call tools provided by other programs. It connects 8 servers in the project configuration and 6 servers in the global configuration. The servers provide model access, event logging, memory search, code search, browser control, media generation, local image generation, and Wikipedia lookup. A watchdog is a small monitoring program that checks whether a service is alive and restarts it when it has stopped.
mechanism: First, the project configuration lists the 8 MCP servers needed for that project. A configuration is a set of settings that tells an AI client which external services it may call.
The global configuration lists 6 shared servers for use outside the project. Keeping a common global set reduces the chance that each client is configured differently.
The model gateway is exposed as an MCP server. A model gateway is a service that sends requests to language or media models while applying shared budgets, caching, and usage records.
The memory and event-log servers store information and tool activity in shared systems. This lets different clients use the same history and makes activity easier to inspect.

The code-search server retrieves relevant parts of the machine's indexed code, while the browser server performs web actions. Each capability remains in its own server so it can be updated or tested separately.

The Wikipedia server handles narrow factual lookups, and the media-generation servers handle remote or local generation tasks. Separating these jobs keeps specialized behavior out of the model gateway.
The watchdog checks the health of the MCP servers. When a server is terminated or otherwise stops responding, the watchdog starts it again without waiting for a person.

The AI client calls the servers through MCP rather than using a different custom integration for each client. This common route matters because budgets, caches, logs, and tool behavior can then be shared.
