systems.name: Five-gate post-render video QA gate with on-screen caption presence and caption-to-script alignment
systems.decision: A rendered video could pass checks on its input files and still contain visible or audible defects in the final file. This system prevents specific shipped failures, including missing or mistimed captions, long silence, missing music, wrong visual content, and repeated frames, by checking the rendered video itself.
systems.what_it_does: This system runs five checks on the completed episode directory and refuses the episode if any check fails. It uses audio and video inspection tools, image-pixel checks, caption timing data, and a vision-capable language model, which is a model that can inspect video and return a structured judgment. It also aligns spoken-word timings with the script so captions use the script's spelling while retaining timing information from the transcription. OCR, or optical character recognition, is used only as an advisory measurement and does not decide whether an episode passes.
mechanism: The gate first locates the rendered video by trying the expected file name and then any MP4 file in the episode directory. This matters because a directory name and a video file name may differ.

Gate 1 checks audio and duration. It uses ffprobe, a tool that reads media properties, to compare the video duration with the voice duration plus the expected call-to-action card. It allows a 3.0 second difference. It also searches for trailing silence longer than 3.5 seconds and refuses the episode when no music bed is present.

Gate 2 checks the caption timing and text data. It compares captions with nine known phonetic transcription errors and refuses the first matching corruption. It also measures the gap between the last caption word and the end of the voice track and refuses a gap greater than 2.0 seconds.

Gate 3 checks burned-in captions in the actual rendered pixels. It samples at the midpoint of each caption word, looks for bright glyph pixels next to dark outline pixels, checks the expected accent colour, and requires at least 1200 glyph pixels on a qualifying frame. At least 80 percent of narration frames must contain a caption. This comes after the caption-track check because a correct text file does not prove that text was visibly drawn into the video.

Gate 4 sends the actual rendered video to a vision model in groups of 6 shots. The model returns a structured judgment for each shot about the subject, narration beat, and orientation. Missing judgments for any shot cause refusal. The model chain tries minimax-m3 first and gemini-3.1-pro-preview second, with different answer budgets based on observed reasoning failures.
Gate 5 checks for repeated frames. It refuses consecutive duplicate frames, any reused frame, or a repeated block where shots 1 to 16 match shots 17 to 32.

Before Gate 2, the alignment stage compares transcription tokens with script tokens using a sequence matcher. It keeps the transcription timings but replaces transcription spelling with the script spelling. If word counts differ, it distributes the original time span across the script words according to word length, and it saves the original transcription separately.

metrics.value: the gate runs 5 checks, refuses the episode if any one of them fails, and exits with a non-zero code so the caller cannot treat a failure as a pass
metrics.explanation: There are five checks. One failed check is enough to refuse the episode. A non-zero exit code is a computer signal meaning the command ended in failure, which prevents a calling process from treating the result as successful.
metrics.proves: The gate has five refusal checks and communicates failure to the calling process.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that each check detects every possible defect or that the caller always handles the non-zero code correctly.

metrics.value: the measured thresholds are 3.5 seconds maximum trailing silence, 3.0 seconds maximum duration delta against voice plus the call to action card, and a 2.0 second maximum gap between the last caption word and the end of the audio
metrics.explanation: The rendered video may have no more than 3.5 seconds of silence at the end. Its duration may differ from voice plus the call-to-action card by no more than 3.0 seconds. The last caption word may end no more than 2.0 seconds before the audio ends.
metrics.proves: These are the explicit refusal thresholds for trailing silence, total duration difference, and caption-ending gap.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the thresholds are perceptually ideal or that shorter gaps and duration differences never indicate a defect.

metrics.value: 9 known transcription phonetic corruptions are refused by name, including Akasa for Akaza and Muzan for Muzan
metrics.explanation: The gate lists nine named transcription mistakes that are refused. The examples show that similar-sounding or incorrectly recognized names can be blocked.
metrics.proves: Nine specific transcription corruption patterns are included in the refusal list.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that all possible transcription mistakes are covered.

metrics.value: 34 anachronism terms are listed as forbidden objects for the era check
metrics.explanation: The system has a list of 34 terms representing objects considered wrong for the episode's historical setting. An anachronism is something shown in a time period where it does not belong.
metrics.proves: Thirty-four forbidden terms are available for the era-related visual check.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the vision model detects every anachronism or that every listed term is found correctly.

metrics.value: run against the rendered Inosuke episode the gate returned FAIL on 2 findings: the MP4 is 39.7 seconds against an expected 44.0 seconds for voice plus call to action, and no music bed was present. The caption, on-screen caption and frame loop gates returned PASS
metrics.explanation: One rendered episode had two failures. Its video was 39.7 seconds long instead of the expected 44.0 seconds, and no music bed file was found. The caption timing, visible-caption, and repeated-frame checks passed for that run.
metrics.proves: The gate detected those two defects and separately passed the three named checks in that run.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the remaining checks passed, that the episode was fixed, or that the same findings occur in all episodes.

metrics.value: run against the rendered Rengoku episode the gate returned FAIL on the same 2 findings: the MP4 is 39.4 seconds against an expected 43.9 seconds, and no music bed was present
metrics.explanation: A second rendered episode was 39.4 seconds instead of the expected 43.9 seconds, and it had no music bed. The two duration figures and the two expected figures are the ones the gate reported.
metrics.proves: The gate detected the same two categories of defect in this second run.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that other checks passed or that all episodes have these defects.

metrics.value: ffprobe confirms the duration finding is real and not a gate arithmetic error. The Rengoku MP4 is 39.366667 seconds and the voice track is 39.851125 seconds, and no music_act*.wav file exists anywhere under the zenpai episode directory. metrics.value: the frame loop gate correctly refused a deliberately duplicated frame sequence: 4 shots on the same frame produced Duplicate frames: {'a.jpg': 4}
metrics.explanation: A test video used the same image for four shots. The gate reported that image four times and refused the sequence.
metrics.proves: The frame loop gate can detect repeated use of the same frame in a controlled test.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that all kinds of visually similar but non-identical loops are detected.

metrics.value: the caption gate correctly refused a truncated caption track: a track ending at 0.5 seconds against 40.0 seconds of audio produced a gap greater than 2 seconds
metrics.explanation: The captions stopped at 0.5 seconds while the audio lasted 40.0 seconds. The resulting gap was far above the 2.0 second limit, so the gate refused the episode.
metrics.proves: The caption timing gate detects a caption track that ends substantially before the audio.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that small timing errors or incorrectly worded captions are always detected.

metrics.value: the Inosuke episode has 17 shots with 17 distinct frames, which is why the frame loop gate passes on it
metrics.explanation: The episode contains 17 shots and each shot points to a different frame. The frame loop check therefore found no reused frame in that list.
metrics.proves: That episode's shot list had 17 distinct frame references.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the frames are visually appropriate, that consecutive frames are sufficiently different, or that the final video contains no repeated encoded frames.

metrics.value: the caption alignment stage rewrote 702 transcribed words into 698 script words across 4 episodes, changing 16 spans
metrics.explanation: Across four episodes, the alignment process changed the caption word list from 702 transcription words to 698 script words and modified 16 groups of words. A span is a contiguous section of text treated as one changed region.
metrics.proves: The alignment stage made the stated number of word and span changes in those four episodes.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that every change was correct or that the new timings match human judgments.

metrics.value: the Genya episode is where the alignment stage earns its place: the transcription heard 'moves on' where the script says 'Muzan', heard 'Muzon' 3 times for 'Muzan', and heard 'niche-in' for 'nichirin'. All of those printed on screen before the stage ran

metrics.proves: The alignment stage addressed concrete caption spelling errors in that episode.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the alignment stage catches every named-entity error or that the corrected text is always semantically right.

metrics.value: the Giyu episode transcript heard 'Hashiro' for 'Hashira' and 'Sanami' for 'Sanemi', and the Rengoku episode heard 'core' for 'corps'. All three were on screen before the alignment stage ran
metrics.explanation: Three additional transcription errors appeared in captions before alignment: Hashiro instead of Hashira, Sanami instead of Sanemi, and core instead of corps.
metrics.proves: The alignment stage had additional real spelling errors to correct in those episodes.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the corrected captions were independently reviewed or that similar errors are absent elsewhere.

metrics.value: the alignment stage keeps timings monotonic and keeps every word inside the file, and writes the pre-alignment transcription to words_whisper.json so the original timings stay recoverable
metrics.explanation: Monotonic timings mean each word starts at or after the previous word rather than moving backward. The stage keeps every word within the audio file and saves the original transcription separately for later comparison.
metrics.proves: The alignment implementation includes timing-order, file-boundary, and original-data preservation rules.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the resulting word boundaries are perceptually accurate.

metrics.value: the visual gate now executes a real model call and refused the rendered Inosuke episode on shot 3. The shot carries the narration 'He taught himself his breathing style by watching how they charged', and the frame on that shot is an empty traditional Japanese interior with no character in it and no animal in it. The frame was opened and looked at, and the finding is right
metrics.explanation: The visual check sent the episode to a model and refused shot 3 because the narration described a character learning by watching animals charge, while the image showed an empty interior with neither a character nor an animal.
metrics.proves: The visual gate can make a refusal based on a mismatch between spoken content and the rendered image, and this finding was manually confirmed.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the model will reliably detect all subject, beat, or orientation problems.

metrics.value: the shots are judged in groups of 6, one model call per group, and a group whose verdicts do not cover every shot in it is a refusal rather than a pass. Asked for 17 verdicts in one call, the model returned a single summary object and used the whole 4000 token budget
metrics.explanation: The system sends no more than six shots in one model request. It requires one result for every shot in that group. A test asking for 17 results produced only one summary and consumed all 4000 allowed output tokens, so grouping is used to reduce incomplete responses.
metrics.proves: The implementation has six-shot grouping and refuses incomplete model coverage.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that six is the optimal group size or that every grouped response is accurate.

metrics.value: one group of 6 shots costs 0.0054 USD at 12287 input tokens and 1468 output tokens, so a 17 shot episode costs about 0.016 USD to check
metrics.explanation: One six-shot model request used 12,287 input tokens and 1,468 output tokens and was recorded at 0.0054 USD. Three such groups are needed for 17 shots, giving an approximate total of 0.016 USD.
metrics.proves: This records the measured cost and token use for one model group and an approximate cost for a 17-shot episode.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove a fixed future price, because model prices, token counts, retries, and group contents can change.

metrics.value: the frame loop gate now reads the episode under test from any working directory. A probe episode with 4 shots on one frame is refused from a working directory that holds no shots.json, and the rendered Inosuke episode passes from a working directory that holds a duplicate frame shot list
metrics.explanation: The gate uses the episode directory supplied to it instead of assuming that the current terminal directory contains the episode files. A controlled test showed that a four-shot repeated frame was refused even when launched elsewhere, and a separate run showed the rendered episode could pass while the current directory contained unrelated shot data.
metrics.proves: The frame loop check reads the intended episode location rather than relying on the launch directory.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that every other gate is independent of the current directory.

metrics.value: the visual gate uses minimax-m3 first, the cheapest model in the registry that declares video in its input modalities, and gemini-3.1-pro-preview second. The model the gate used before, qwen3-vl-235b, cannot take a video at all, so the file has to go through the video argument rather than the image argument
metrics.explanation: The visual gate first tries minimax-m3 and then gemini-3.1-pro-preview. The first model is selected as the least expensive registered option that accepts video. The previously used qwen3-vl-235b model does not accept video input, so the rendered file must be sent through a video input field rather than as a still image.
metrics.proves: The model order and input type were chosen using declared video-input support and cost information.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the cheapest model is the most accurate or that the fallback is always available.

metrics.value: the cheap video model still burns its answer budget on reasoning about one live call in five, even with reasoning turned off. The failed call spent the whole 4000 token budget and returned no output, and the gateway logged it as a reasoning burn. The second model in the chain exists because of that measurement
metrics.explanation: In one out of five live calls in the measured sample, the cheaper model used all 4000 output tokens for internal reasoning and returned no usable answer, even though reasoning was disabled in the request.
metrics.proves: The measured sample contained a serious incomplete-response failure and motivated the fallback model.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not establish a permanent one-in-five failure rate or explain whether the rate changes with different videos.

metrics.value: the second model needs a larger answer budget than the first. At 4000 tokens it wrote 3996 tokens and never reached the JSON array, and at 12000 tokens it returned a clean 6 object verdict array on a live call
metrics.explanation: The fallback model failed to finish its structured answer with a 4000-token limit, using 3996 tokens before the required array. With a 12000-token limit, it returned six verdict objects as required for a six-shot group.
metrics.proves: The larger answer budget resolved the observed incomplete-response case for that live call.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that 12000 tokens will always produce valid output or that the extra budget improves visual accuracy.

metrics.value: the rendered file is found by one resolver used by every gate, trying the directory name first and then any mp4 in the episode folder. EP_INOSUKE lives in ep_inosuke, so the exact name never matches and the fallback is what finds the file
metrics.explanation: A shared file resolver first tries a file name based on the episode directory and then searches for an MP4 in that directory. In the cited example, the exact name did not match, so the fallback search located the rendered video.
metrics.proves: All gates use a common fallback strategy for locating the rendered MP4.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the fallback always selects the correct file when a directory contains multiple MP4 files.

metrics.value: the trailing silence check measures the rendered file now. Before the fix, ffmpeg was pointed at a path rebuilt from the directory name that did not exist, and the parser required the silence start and the silence end on one line while ffmpeg prints them on separate lines, so the value stayed at zero on every episode
metrics.explanation: The silence check previously examined an invalid reconstructed file path and expected ffmpeg output in the wrong layout. Because of those two problems, it reported zero silence for every episode. The fix makes it inspect the actual rendered file and handle separate silence-start and silence-end lines.
metrics.proves: The earlier zero values were caused by file-location and output-parsing defects, and the check was changed to address them.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not provide a measured before-and-after accuracy rate for silence detection.

metrics.value: the on-screen caption check found the defect it was built for. A copy of the Rengoku episode with the captions stripped out passes the caption track gate because words.json is untouched, and fails the on-screen caption gate with 0 of 40 narration frames captioned
metrics.explanation: A test copy removed visible caption pixels but left the caption timing file unchanged. The text-file check passed because its input was unchanged, while the pixel check found zero captioned frames out of 40.
metrics.proves: The on-screen pixel check detects missing burned-in captions that a caption-track check alone cannot detect.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the pixel check detects every styling, spelling, or partial-caption defect.

metrics.value: the on-screen caption check passes on every real render tested: 40 of 40 narration frames captioned on the Rengoku episode, 40 of 40 on the Inosuke episode, and 40 of 40 on the anime hive render
metrics.explanation: For each of the three tested real renders, all 40 sampled narration frames met the pixel criteria for containing a visible caption.
metrics.proves: Those three tested renders met the measured visible-caption coverage rule.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that captions are spelled correctly, readable at every moment, or correct on untested renders.

metrics.value: the on-screen caption check was confirmed by eye as well as by the script. The Rengoku frame at 5.0 seconds shows the phrase AND HE DID with DID in yellow, the stripped copy at the same timestamp shows the black bar with no text, and the anime hive frame at the word midpoint 5.61 seconds shows MADARA in red
metrics.explanation: Manual inspection agreed with the automated pixel check. One frame showed expected text and colour, the stripped comparison showed the empty caption background, and another channel showed its expected red caption.
metrics.proves: The automated result matched visual inspection for these sampled frames.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that manual inspection was performed for every frame or every episode.

metrics.value: the on-screen caption check is channel aware and refuses a cross-channel mismatch. The anime hive profile against the zenpai render reached 42 percent coverage and the zenpai profile against the anime hive render reached 0 percent, both below the 80 percent floor
metrics.explanation: Using the wrong channel profile caused only 42 percent coverage in one direction and 0 percent in the other. Both results were below the required 80 percent coverage, so the mismatches were refused.
metrics.proves: The gate can distinguish the tested channel caption positions and colours and can reject a cross-channel profile.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that the profiles remain correct after future builder changes.

metrics.value: the caption band and the caption colours are measured from the builders, not guessed. The zenpai builder draws at 0.667 of the frame height with a 5 pixel black stroke, and the anime hive builder draws at 0.78 of the frame height with a 16 pixel stroke, and the rendered frames were opened and checked against those constants
metrics.explanation: The caption band is the vertical area where captions are expected. One builder places captions at 0.667 of frame height with a 5 pixel black outline, while the other places them at 0.78 of frame height with a 16 pixel outline. Rendered frames were inspected against those settings.
metrics.proves: The profiles use measured builder settings rather than arbitrary guesses for the tested channels.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that all caption colours, sizes, or future builder versions are covered.

metrics.value: the OCR text match stays advisory because the measurement says so. The masked OCR containment hit rate was 73.2 percent for zenpai and 21.4 percent for the anime hive, and a tight bounding box made it worse at 65.9 percent and 11.9 percent, so a text mismatch cannot refuse an episode without producing false refusals on correct ones
metrics.explanation: OCR matched the expected text in 73.2 percent of one channel's cases and 21.4 percent of the other's. Restricting OCR to a tighter region reduced the rates to 65.9 percent and 11.9 percent. Because correct captions were missed often, OCR is not used as a refusal rule.
metrics.proves: The measured OCR approach was too unreliable to serve as a hard pass or fail condition in these tests.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that a different OCR engine, image treatment, or language setting would perform the same way.

metrics.value: the gate's own docstring used to claim that the visual gate checked caption styling against the brief. No check read the caption pixels and no check looked at a banner, so the claim was false. An abstract syntax tree parse of the old gate confirmed that the caption gate and the frame loop gate never touched the MP4, and the caption-stripped copy passed the caption gate
metrics.explanation: The old documentation claimed a visual caption-style check, but the old code did not inspect rendered pixels or the banner. A program-structure inspection confirmed that the relevant old checks did not open the MP4, and a caption-stripped test passed the old caption gate.
metrics.proves: The previous implementation did not enforce the caption-pixel behavior described in its documentation.
metrics.does_not_prove: It does not prove that every other old documented behavior was false or that the new implementation has no similar documentation gaps.

systems.honest_limit: The five-gate system measures selected audio, caption, pixel, model, and frame-loop failures, but it does not measure every possible visual or semantic defect. OCR is intentionally advisory because its measured hit rates are weak. The vision model can fail to return complete results, and the evidence includes live-call failures and model-budget adjustments. The reported costs and pass results come from particular tests, not a universal accuracy or price guarantee. The source does not provide a complete human-labeled benchmark, recall, precision, F1 score, or independent measurement of all gate errors.
systems.status_note: Five checks refuse an episode when one check fails.
